artifact.title: AWS announces AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Equinix
artifact.summary: AWS Interconnect - last mile is now available in preview with Equinix. You can connect your infrastructure across Equinix's global network of 282 data centers worldwide to AWS in a few clicks. Interconnect - last mile gives you managed, private, and resilient connections to AWS, so you don't have to order cross-connects or configure routers. To set up in the AWS Management Console, choose an AWS Region, a bandwidth speed, a Direct Connect gateway, and your Equinix Fabric One project ID. AWS generates an activation key, which you enter in the Equinix Fabric One portal to complete the setup. You can also initiate the connection from the Equinix Fabric One portal. AWS and Equinix set up quad-redundant capacity in advance, across two locations and four separate links, with BGP peering, VLANs and ASNs configured for you. Every connection is built for maximum resilience and comes with a 99.99% availability SLA. Traffic between AWS and Equinix edge devices is encrypted with MACsec by default. During the preview, you can order 1 Gbps Interconnect - last mile connections at no charge to the US West (N. California) Region through the San Jose metro and to the US East (N. Virginia) Region through the Northern Virginia metro. When Interconnect - last mile with Equinix becomes generally available, you'll be able to scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps in the console. You can create connections using the console, the AWS CLI, or the API. Partners can integrate using the open API package

artifact.title: US Data Centre Boom Adds 54 GW to Pipeline, Raising RE Demand
artifact.summary: The US data centre development pipeline expanded by 54 GW in the second quarter of 2026, marking a 29% increase year-on-year as developers accelerated construction amid growing concerns over power availability, according to a new report by Wood Mackenzie. The expansion is expected to intensify the focus on electricity supply, grid infrastructure and clean energy procurement as data centres emerge as a major source of incremental power demand in the US. The cumulative disclosed data centre pipeline has crossed 430 GW, with around 59% of the capacity under active development. Nearly 80 GW of projects were under construction, up from 44 GW at the end of the first quarter, Wood Mackenzie said in its US data centre pipeline report. The pipeline added 5% capacity quarter-on-quarter. Meanwhile, utility commitments backed by signed electricity service or construction agreements reached 201 GW, equivalent to 26% of projected US peak electricity demand in 2026. However, the rapid expansion is facing mounting opposition from local communities and lawmakers. artifact.title: Can US Interconnection Queues Survive Data Center-Driven Load Growth?
artifact.summary: In ERCOT, 198 GW of large load applied for interconnection in Q1 2026 alone, with 86 GW of new load requests under review roughly equal to ERCOT's current peak load. PJM is grappling with a capacity shortfall that could reach 15 GW by 2030 as new load additions outpace new generation, underscoring that large-load interconnection rules were designed for a fundamentally different era.

artifact.title: Stretching the Possibilities: Where Large-Load Tariffs Fit in the Future of Data Center Flexibility
artifact.summary: As of Q2 2026, utilities had proposed 25 new large-load tariffs and service rules, with 45% specifying a 50 MW peak demand threshold — consistent with FERC's June 2026 show-cause order definitions — and one-quarter now including concrete dispatchable large-load flexibility or curtailment pathways. State examples include Pennsylvania's model 50 MW+ interruptible tariff tied to PJM's Emergency Load Response Program and Xcel Energy's (MN) 100 MW+ optional curtailment rate.

artifact.title: FERC Interconnection Reform 2026: EPC Guide
artifact.summary: FERC is running two parallel interconnection reform tracks in 2026: a multi-year generation-side reform under Order 2023—where PJM's compliance plan was only partially accepted in April 2026 and actual timelines now exceed eight years—and a faster, aggressive load-side track for data centers moving in months. The national interconnection backlog stands at roughly 2,200 GW, with a live cost-allocation question opened at FERC in June 2026 that could materially change who pays for network upgrades triggered by large-load projects.
